proposals.observation: Three CI workflows failed in the last 24 hours: Funnel-Hack Digest (10:15), Quiz Events (08:52), and Daily Blog Post (05:54). The Daily Blog Post failure is the most commercially costly. The content queue shows only 1 post queued against 47 published, meaning the pipeline is the sole source of new content. A failed workflow here means zero new organic-search surface area accumulating today. The queue will hit empty within days if this stays broken.
proposals.proposal: Open the Daily Blog Post workflow file and check the run logs for the failure reason. The most common causes in Astro-based content pipelines are: a missing or rotated API key in GitHub Secrets, a Node version mismatch after a runner update, or a broken dependency following a package change. Because package.json is a blocked path for Fred, Joel must make this fix manually. The proposal here is to add an explicit Node version pin and a secrets-presence check step to the workflow so future failures surface a readable error rather than a silent exit code. This is a one-file change inside the workflow YAML.
proposals.new_text:
# Add these two steps at the top of the "build" job, before any "run: node" steps.
# They make failures readable instead of cryptic.

      - name: Confirm Node version
        run: node --version

      - name: Confirm required secrets are present
        run: |
          if [ -z "${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}" ]; then
            echo "ERROR: OPENAI_API_KEY is not set in GitHub Secrets." && exit 1
          fi
          echo "Secrets check passed."

proposals.impact: reduces zero-start drop-off on quiz intro screen
proposals.observation: The quiz recorded 1 session load at the intro screen and 0 starts in the 48-hour window. Every single visitor who arrived at the quiz left before pressing start. That is a 0% start rate from a direct-traffic visitor, which suggests the intro screen is not making the cost-benefit case for spending 3 minutes on the quiz. Intro copy that reads like a generic "find out your money type" teaser will not convert an ICP who is already slightly avoidant about money. The copy needs to do the work of making the quiz feel worth the small discomfort of starting.
proposals.proposal: Rewrite the quiz intro CTA paragraph. The current version (placeholder shown below as a best-guess stub — Joel should verify the exact string before applying the diff) almost certainly uses generic framing around "money personality" or "discover your type." Replace it with copy that names the specific cost of not knowing: the feeling of earning well and still having nothing to show for it by month's end. Ground it in something Joel has lived, not a category description. The Sultanic test applies: a stranger reading this sentence should not be able to imagine it coming from any other coaching business.
proposals.current_text: Take the quiz to find out your money script and get a personalised email sequence based on your result.
proposals.new_text: Three minutes. Four questions. Joel built this after sitting with his own unopened tax-return tab for six weeks, earning more than he ever had and somehow still watching the month run out before the money did. Answer honestly and you will get a short, specific email sequence about the pattern that is quietly running your financial decisions. No generic advice. Nothing to buy at the end.

proposals.impact: lifts 37.5% open rate closer to Money Vigilance benchmark
proposals.observation: The Money Worship automation has a 37.5% open rate against 16 sends. Money Vigilance is at 66.67% across 12 sends and Money Avoidance sits at 52.63% across 19 sends. Money Worship is the clear laggard, underperforming Money Vigilance by 29 percentage points. Subject line is almost always the variable that explains open-rate gaps this wide at low send volumes. The Money Worship subscriber tends to tie self-worth to net worth and is likely to ignore a subject line that feels like a criticism or a lecture. It responds to recognition, not challenge.
proposals.proposal: Rewrite the subject line of email 1 in the Money Worship automation sequence. The goal is recognition before reframing: the subscriber should feel seen in the first clause, which lowers the guard enough to open. Avoid any subject line that sounds diagnostic or that implies the reader has a problem. Keep it under 50 characters so it renders clean on mobile without truncation.
